newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn to exceed EMU deficit but qualify - Ifo.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn to exceed EMU deficit but qualify - Ifo.

text.p: The Ifo economic institute on Thursday said Germany's 1997 budget deficit would exceed the Maastricht Treaty ceiling but this would not prevent it from qualifying for economic and monetary union (EMU).
Ifo said Germany's overall state budget deficit would be just under 120 billion marks ($69 billion), or 3.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year.

In a speech prepared for the institute's annual meeting, Ifo President Karl-Heinrich Oppenlaender said, however, that this forecast did not take into account new saving measures being discussed by Bonn.

"According to our forecast, which is subject to considerable uncertainties, Germany will not meet the Maastricht reference target for the deficit ratio -- that is without the savings measures that are currently being planned in Bonn," Oppenlaender said.
The Maastricht Treaty sets a ceiling of three percent for the deficit to GDP ratio of countries wishing to join the single currency, scheduled to start in January 1999.
With high unemployment levels draining funds from German government coffers, many independent analysts have said this target is very unlikely to be met.

"I nevertheless believe that with such a deficit, Germany will not be denied entry to European monetary union since the Maastricht Treaty allows certain divergence from the reference target," Oppenlaender said.
"The public has the impression that even small decimal point divergences from the three percent level would endanger the stability of the future currency. This is wrong," he said.
"We should, therefore, end the decimal point discussion about this year's deficit as quickly as possible."
Oppenlaender also warned Bonn against emergency or one-off measures, saying these were unnecessary and dangerous for credibility.

Commenting on the recent clash between Bonn and the Bundesbank over government plans to revalue and take a pay-out from central bank gold reserves, Oppenlaeder said the battle had severely damaged the confidence of finanical markets.
"The confidence of financial markets in the sustainablity of budget consolidation has declined considerably," he said.
"Short-term measures to meet Maastricht Treaty reference targets at any price can destroy trust more than they can encourage it."

The Ifo president said the stability of the euro currency was far more dependent on the monetary policy conducted by the European Central Bank (ECB) in 1999 and called for sustainable and solid fiscal policy to make that job easier.

But he cautioned against political intervention in foreign exchange markets to try to influence the future euro's echange rate against the dollar, saying this could inflict considerable damage on the monetary policy of the ECB.
"Politicians should concentrate first and foremost on achieving budgetary consolidation," Oppenlaender said. -- Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.731 German Marks)
